home.title: Know your crop's grade and fair price before you sell.
home.lede: Take a photo of your dates, melons or grain. Dera Mandi grades it, shows what buyers pay for that grade, and finds buyers, storage and transport near you.

about.title: How Dera Mandi works
about.lede: A tool for growers in Dera Ismail Khan to know what their crop is worth before they sell it.
about.problem1: D.I. Khan grows export-grade Dhakki dates and Kulachi melons, along with wheat and sugarcane. The value leaks out before it reaches the grower, for three linked reasons.
about.problemPrice: Price is opaque. Most growers sell to a commission agent at the local mandi, under time pressure, at the price the agent names.
about.problemSpoil: Fruit spoils. There is little cold storage and the road to Multan or Karachi is long, so fruit is sold fast and cheap, or rots.
about.problemLots: Small lots cannot reach export. One grower rarely has enough graded fruit to interest an exporter, so the export premium goes to middlemen.
about.steps1: The grower photographs the crop and enters the quantity and village.
about.steps2: The app grades it A, B or C and shows today's fair price for that grade, from public mandi rates, and whether to sell now, send it to Multan, or store it.
about.steps3: It lists buyers who take that crop, grade and quantity, and nearby storage and transport, with cold storage first for fruit.
about.steps4: The grower picks a buyer and sends a request on WhatsApp, with a grade certificate to show.
about.gradeTitle: How the grade is worked out
about.grade1: For khajoor, the grade comes from an image model (MobileNetV2) trained on {{trained}} photos of graded Pakistani khajoor from a public dataset. On {{tested}} photos of the three-grade varieties that it had never seen, it gave the right grade {{accuracy}}% of the time (95% range {{low}} to {{high}}%). Always guessing the most common grade would score {{baseline}}%. On a khajoor variety it never trained on (Fasli Toto, all labelled Grade 1), it said A for {{unseenA}}% of them. It runs on the phone; photos are never uploaded.
about.grade2: Its limits, plainly: the dataset shows Gajar, Kupro and Aseel khajoor, photographed one fruit at a time under a ring light. It has no Dhakki, and no piles photographed in a field, so accuracy on real field photos will be lower until Dhakki photos are added. Middle grade (B) is the hardest for it. The crop is still checked in person before anything is shipped.
about.grade3: Sugarcane is graded by a model trained on photos of good and damaged cane billets (82% per photo on held-out photos, 93% when several photos of one piece are combined). Melon uses a model trained on other graded fruit, because no graded melon photos exist; it has never been tested on a melon. Wheat and other crops get a rule-based estimate from colour, size and visible spots, not a trained model. If a photo is too dark, washed out, or does not show the crop, the app asks for a retake instead of guessing.
about.grade4: Next step: collect 100 to 300 graded Dhakki photos from D.I. Khan growers and retrain the same model on them.
about.lots1: Dera Mandi's plan is to combine nearby lots of the same crop and grade until they reach the size an exporter buys. In this prototype, that shows as a note on the result screen when a lot is too small.
about.realTitle: What is real in this prototype
about.real1: Real: the full listing flow, the trained grade models for khajoor, sugarcane and melon, photo checks, today's public mandi rates (AMIS Punjab), the sell or store comparison, the certificate, matching by crop, grade, quantity and distance, and history, in Urdu and English, with a spoken voice guide.
about.real2: Sample: every buyer, store and transporter is an invented sample provider, not a real business, and their offers are scaled to today's rate. In demo mode a request opens WhatsApp to the team's demo number, not to a buyer.
about.real3: Your listings and photos are kept only in this phone's browser. Nothing is uploaded.
about.faq1q: What if a grower cannot read or has no smartphone?
about.faq1a: The app opens in Urdu, can speak every step aloud (tap the screen twice), uses large simple steps and crop pictures, and needs no account. In helper mode, one literate helper in a village can list crops for many growers from one phone.
about.faq2q: Why trust a grade from a photo?
about.faq2a: The photos stay with the listing so anyone can check them, and the crop is inspected in person before shipment. The grade is a fair starting point for the conversation, not a final verdict.
about.faq3q: Cold storage barely exists in D.I. Khan.
about.faq3a: True. Pooling demand from many growers is what makes shared storage worth building, and meanwhile the app routes toward existing cold hubs in Multan and Karachi.
about.team: Built for Imaginathon by Banao by The Four Musketeers.
about.credit: Training data: Maitlo, A. K. et al., Date Fruit Dataset for Inspection and Grading, Mendeley Data, V3 (2023), doi:10.17632/s5zfvsw5kv.3, licensed CC BY 4.0. Only the original photos were used; duplicates were removed and photos were cropped and resized for training and for the in-app samples. Sugarcane: The77Lab (LSU AgCenter), SugarcaneDeepLearning billet images (no licence published; non-commercial prototype use with attribution). Melon stand-in: AFruitDB, Mendeley Data bz65dz2pbj, CC BY 4.0. Prices: AMIS Punjab (amis.pk).
about.grade1Dhakki: For khajoor, the grade comes from an image model (MobileNetV2) trained on {{trained}} graded khajoor photos: a public Pakistani dataset plus Dhakki photographed and graded in D.I. Khan. On {{tested}} Dhakki photos it had never seen, it gave the right grade {{accuracy}}% of the time (95% range {{low}} to {{high}}%). Always guessing the most common grade would score {{baseline}}%. It runs on the phone; photos are never uploaded.
about.grade2Dhakki: Its limits, plainly: the Dhakki test set is small ({{tested}} photos), so the true accuracy could sit anywhere in that range. Its training photos show one fruit at a time on a plain background, so piles and field light may score lower. Middle grade (B) is the hardest for it. The crop is still checked in person before anything is shipped.

cropModel.kernelsTitle: What the wheat model saw in {{count}} kernels
cropModel.card_wheat_kernel_class: Each kernel was checked by an image model trained on {{trained}} photos of single wheat kernels. Tested on {{tested}} kernels it had never seen, cut out on a cloth the way the app does, it named the exact kernel type {{accuracy}}% of the time (likely range {{low}} to {{high}}%), and put the kernel in the right quality group (sound, minor or serious damage) {{group}}% of the time.
cropModel.card_binary_good_damaged: Graded by an image model trained on {{trained}} photos of sugarcane billets marked good or damaged. On {{tested}} billets it had never seen, it was right {{accuracy}}% of the time (likely range {{low}} to {{high}}%). It only knows good and damaged, so it gives A or C, never B.
cropModel.card_grade3_proxy: Graded by an image model trained on {{trained}} graded photos of other fruit (mango, papaya, apple, tomato, Burmese grape). On {{tested}} fruit photos it had never seen, it gave the right grade {{accuracy}}% of the time (likely range {{low}} to {{high}}%).
cropModel.wheatRule: Lot rule we use: Grade A needs at least 90% sound kernels and at most 2% seriously damaged; B at least 75% sound and at most 8% seriously damaged; anything worse is C.
cropModel.melonProxy: No public dataset of graded melons exists, so this model learned from other graded fruit and has never been tested on melons. Treat the grade as a rough guide until it is retrained on Kulachi melon photos.
cropModel.card_group: When all photos of one billet were combined, as the app does, it was right {{groupAcc}}% of the time over {{groupCount}} billets (likely range {{groupLow}} to {{groupHigh}}%).

advice.title: What we noticed in the photo
advice.patches: Dark, grey or green patches cover {{v}} of the produce
advice.lotMix: The lot is mixed: {{b}} fruits came out B and {{c}} came out C
advice.tip_dhakki_dates_A: Keep this lot together and sell it as Grade A. Show the certificate: buyers pay for grade they can trust.
advice.tip_dhakki_dates_B: Pick out the torn, dry or light-coloured fruit. The better fruit may then sell as Grade A, and the rest separately.
advice.tip_dhakki_dates_C: Sell soon and locally. Cold storage will not raise the grade of damaged fruit, and it keeps costing money.
advice.tip_kulachi_melon_A: Melons do not keep: sell within days, and ask for the upper end of the band.
advice.tip_kulachi_melon_B: Separate the cracked or bruised melons. Sound ones fetch more when they are not mixed with damaged ones.
advice.tip_kulachi_melon_C: Sell today at the local mandi. Every day now costs more than any better price.
advice.tip_wheat_A: Clean grain earns the top rate. Keep it dry in bags off the floor until it is sold.
advice.tip_wheat_B: Sieving out broken kernels and dust can move the lot up a grade.
advice.tip_wheat_C: Clean out mouldy grain, stones and chaff first, and keep damp grain apart. Mould spreads in storage.
advice.tip_sugarcane_A: Get it to the mill within a day of cutting: cane loses sugar and weight every day it waits.
advice.tip_sugarcane_B: Strip dry leaves and trim damaged ends before weighing at the mill.
advice.tip_sugarcane_C: Cut out damaged or red-rotted pieces before weighing. Mills can dock the whole load for them.
advice.tip_other_A: Keep the best produce together and show the grade to buyers.
advice.tip_other_B: Sort out the damaged pieces. The rest may then sell as Grade A.
advice.tip_other_C: Sell soon and locally; storing will not improve it.

accuracy.title: How sure are we?
accuracy.intro: Each grade comes from an image model trained on public photo collections. Below is how often each one was right on photos it never saw while learning, and what it has never seen.
accuracy.howTested: How we tested: photos were split before training, near-identical photos were kept together, and the test photos were used once, at the end. The likely range is a 95% interval: with more test photos it would narrow.
accuracy.headline: right on {{n}} test photos it never saw
accuracy.baseline: Always guessing the most common answer would score {{b}}%.
accuracy.recallTitle: When the real answer was this, it said so:
accuracy.kernelGroup: For the lot grade, what matters is the quality group of each kernel (sound, minor or serious damage): it got that right {{acc}}% of the time.
accuracy.rules: Wheat and other crops get a rule-based estimate from colour, coverage and dark spots in the photo. It is not a trained model and its accuracy has not been measured.
accuracy.limits_dhakki_dates: No Dhakki photos: it learned from Gajar, Kupro and Aseel dates. On a variety it had never seen it still gave grades, so treat a Dhakki grade as a guide until Dhakki photos are added.
accuracy.limits_wheat: It learned from close-up scanner photos of single kernels. A phone photo of a handful is coarser, and accuracy on phone photos has not been measured yet.
accuracy.limits_sugarcane: It learned from Louisiana cane varieties photographed on a dark background, and it only knows good or damaged. Local varieties and a sugar test at the mill are not covered.
accuracy.limits_kulachi_melon: No graded melon photos exist in public, so it learned from mango, papaya, apple, tomato and Burmese grape. It has never been tested on a melon.
accuracy.recallAll: Per grade, over all {{n}} test photos (Aseel included):
accuracy.headlineProxy: right on {{n}} test photos of other graded fruit (never tested on melon)
accuracy.wheatTried: We did train a wheat model that checks each kernel: on 2,003 held-out kernels cut out the way the app does, the best run named the kernel type 87% of the time. But on test handfuls it read clean grain as damaged too often to grade a whole lot, so it is not used yet.
